units.text: Let's begin with a puzzle: when was Luxembourg born?
Some people say 1815, when the Grand Duchy was created at the Congress of Vienna.
Others say 1839, when its modern borders were drawn in London.
Others point to 1867, when the great powers guaranteed its independence.
But the story we are telling really starts in the year nine sixty-three, with an exchange of land beside a river.
And before that exchange, there are thousands of years we should not skip.
Our first character has no name.
Archaeologists call him Loschbour man, after the rock shelter near the village of Heffingen where his skeleton was found in 1935.
He lived about eight thousand years ago, when this land was covered in dense forest and people survived by hunting, fishing and gathering.
When scientists sequenced his DNA, decades after his discovery, the result made headlines.
It suggested that this early European had dark skin and blue eyes, a combination that overturned a lot of assumptions about what the first Europeans looked like.
After Loschbour man came farmers, who arrived from the southeast and cleared fields along the river valleys.
Then came the age of metal, first bronze and later iron.
By the last centuries before Christ, the land of Luxembourg belonged to a Celtic people called the Treveri.
The Treveri left a remarkable monument: a fortified hilltop town called the Titelberg, in the far southwest of today's country, close to the French border.
It sat on a high plateau, with ramparts around it, and it was a center for metalworking and trade.
Imagine a town of craftsmen and warriors, with a view across the countryside, and one of the richest cavalry traditions in Gaul.
Then Rome arrived. The first written reference to this territory comes from Julius Caesar himself, in his account of the Gallic Wars.
Around the middle of the first century before Christ, Caesar fought the Treveri, and after years of rebellion and repression, the region was swallowed into the Roman Empire.
The Romans founded a city on the Moselle river, just across what is now the German border: Augusta Treverorum, today's Trier.
Within a few generations it became one of the great cities of the western empire.
At one point it was the home of emperors, and its Roman gates and baths still stand.
The land that would become Luxembourg was Trier's backyard.
It was farmland and forest, crossed by Roman roads and dotted with country estates.
One of those roads ran from the city of Reims, in what is now France, to Trier.
Along it, near today's village of Dalheim, grew a small Roman town with a theater.
At Echternach and at Diekirch, wealthy landowners built grand villas.
At Diekirch, a Roman mosaic from one of those houses survives, laid out in colored stone.
Life was settled, Latin-speaking and, for a few centuries, secure.
Then the empire cracked. In the third and fourth centuries, raiders pushed across the Rhine, and Roman power along the frontier began to wear away.
By the end of the fifth century, the region had passed to the Franks, a Germanic people whose king, Clovis, was building a new kingdom out of the ruins of Roman Gaul.
Luxembourg's land became part of the Frankish heartland, in the eastern half that was later called Austrasia.
Christianity came with the Franks, and with a handful of remarkable missionaries.
The most important for our story is a monk named Willibrord, born in Northumbria, in England, and trained in Ireland.
He crossed the sea to preach to the pagan Frisians, and in the year six ninety-eight he founded a monastery at Echternach, on land given to him by a noblewoman from the Trier area.
Willibrord died in 739 and was buried there.
Echternach became one of the great intellectual centers of medieval Europe.
Its monks copied and illuminated manuscripts so beautiful that they are treasured today in museums in Germany.
And the town still marks its founder's memory with a custom that has lasted for centuries.
Every year, on the Tuesday after Pentecost, thousands of people dance through the streets of Echternach in a procession, hopping in time to a simple polka-like tune, in honor of Saint Willibrord.
UNESCO now recognizes it as part of humanity's living cultural heritage.
Now we move to Charlemagne. In the late 700s and early 800s, the Frankish kings became emperors, and the Echternach region sat comfortably inside their realm.

But when Charlemagne's empire was split among his grandsons by the Treaty of Verdun in eight forty-three, the land that would become Luxembourg fell into the middle kingdom, named after the grandson Lothar.
That middle kingdom did not last.

Over the following decades, it broke up, and the region we are talking about became a borderland, a long-contested strip between the western Frankish kingdom, which would become France, and the eastern Frankish kingdom, which would become Germany.
Then, in the year nine sixty-two, in Rome, a German king named Otto was crowned emperor.
His realm would later be known as the Holy Roman Empire.
It was a loose, shifting collection of kingdoms, duchies, counties and church lands that would last for more than eight hundred years.
And just one year later, a count named Siegfried made a small land deal that no one at the time could have thought important.
Siegfried belonged to a noble family from the Moselle and Ardennes region, and according to tradition he had Carolingian blood.
What he wanted was a stronghold.
On the edge of lands he controlled, there was a rocky promontory rising above the river Alzette, with the ruins of an old fortification.
That fortification belonged to the abbey of Saint Maximin in Trier.
Siegfried offered other lands in exchange, and the monks agreed.
The charter that records the swap, dated 963, gives the name of the place: Lucilinburhuc.
It means roughly little castle.
In time, the name would shorten and soften into Luxembourg.
The rock itself would later be known as the Bock.
Siegfried built a real fortress on it, and from there his family would spread out across the surrounding land.
The place was so well chosen that, as we will see, armies would fight over it for the next nine hundred years.
A legend adds a touch of magic.
It says that Siegfried married a mermaid named Melusina, who agreed to live with him on the condition that he never look at her on a certain day.
He broke the promise, and she vanished beneath the waters of the Alzette, leaving him alone.
Locals say she can still be seen once every seven years, spinning at the bottom of the river.
But the real story is better than the legend.
Because from this small rocky outcrop, Siegfried's descendants would rise to the heights of European power.
They would sit on the throne of Bohemia and wear the imperial crown.
In the next chapter, we meet the House of Luxembourg.
